RESULT — Median wealth comparison, NLSY79 (1985–1996), executed analysis

## Headline finding (deliverable hypothesis)

**Hypothesis (natural language, data-grounded):** Among NLSY79 youth respondents, the median family net wealth of non-Black non-Hispanic ("white"-proxy) individuals was higher than that of Black and Hispanic individuals in every wealth wave from 1985 onward, and the disparity widened dramatically over time. In 1985 the white median was $3,500 vs. $1,600 for Black and $500 for Hispanic respondents (white/Black ratio 2.2×; white/Hispanic 7.0×; gaps $1,900 and $3,000). By 1996 the white median had grown to $42,600 while the Black median reached only $9,800 and the Hispanic median only $2,562 (white/Black ratio 4.4×; white/Hispanic 16.6×; gaps $32,800 and $40,038). Thus the dollar gap roughly multiplied ten-fold between 1985 and 1996, and the relative white–Hispanic disparity more than doubled. Both cohorts' medians grew in absolute terms, but white median wealth grew far faster, so cohort-3 households held roughly 4× the median wealth of Black households and ~17× that of Hispanic households by 1996. This pattern holds in a balanced-panel sensitivity (1985→1996 white/Black ratio 2.4×→4.7×; white/Hispanic 12.7×→17.8×) and in a positives-only median sensitivity, indicating it is not an artifact of negative/zero net worth or of panel attrition direction. Key caveats: cohort 3 is "non-Black non-Hispanic," not strictly white; medians are unweighted sample medians (Black/Hispanic oversamples are built into the design and no survey weights exist in the file); 1996 missingness is high and differential (52.6% missing for cohort 3 vs. ~32% for Black/Hispanic), though the balanced-panel check supports the widening-gap conclusion; wealth is family (respondent/spouse household) level; extreme wealth is top-coded (affects means, not medians).

## Table 1 — Primary medians (unweighted, available case, negatives/zeros kept)

| Wave | Cohort | n | Median | Mean | %neg | %zero |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | Non-Black non-Hisp | 5,774 | $3,500 | $15,201 | 12.6 | 6.6 |
| 1985 | Black | 1,699 | $1,600 | $7,728 | 10.8 | 17.7 |
| 1985 | Hispanic | 2,631 | $500 | $4,920 | 10.9 | 31.0 |
| 1990 | Non-Black non-Hisp | 5,336 | $12,972 | $52,387 | 12.5 | 4.0 |
| 1990 | Black | 1,528 | $4,800 | $27,220 | 15.4 | 10.1 |
| 1990 | Hispanic | 2,431 | $1,600 | $13,394 | 14.3 | 19.5 |
| 1996 | Non-Black non-Hisp | 3,557 | $42,600 | $114,353 | 8.5 | 2.4 |
| 1996 | Black | 1,368 | $9,800 | $45,080 | 10.7 | 10.1 |
| 1996 | Hispanic | 2,114 | $2,562.50 | $22,213 | 12.4 | 22.4 |

## Table 2 — Gaps and ratios (white cohort as reference)

| Wave | White−Black gap | White/Black ratio | White−Hispanic gap | White/Hispanic ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | $1,900 | 2.19× | $3,000 | 7.00× |
| 1990 | $8,172 | 2.70× | $11,372 | 8.11× |
| 1996 | $32,800 | 4.35× | $40,037.50 | 16.62× |

## Table 3 — Balanced-panel sensitivity (n=5,739 in all three waves)

| Wave | White | Black | Hispanic |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | $3,800 | $1,600 | $300 |
| 1990 | $14,750 | $4,100 | $1,200 |
| 1996 | $42,600 | $9,075 | $2,400 |

Panel gaps/ratios: white−Black $2,200 (2.38×) → $10,650 (3.60×) → $33,525 (4.69×); white−Hispanic $3,500 (12.67×) → $13,550 (12.29×) → $40,200 (17.75×). **The widening-gap trajectory holds in the balanced panel** — the same conclusion, with slightly larger ratios, so differential attrition does not drive the finding (dropping 1996 non-respondents does not close the gap; if anything the panel ratios are larger).

## Table 4 — Positives-only median (exclude negatives & zeros)

| Wave | White | Black | Hispanic |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | $5,600 | $3,528 | $2,500 |
| 1990 | $19,900 | $10,700 | $4,800 |
| 1996 | $53,300 | $19,796 | $10,300 |

Robustness: excluding non-positive wealth shrinks the ratios (1996: 2.7× white/Black, 5.2× white/Hispanic) because Hispanic respondents have the highest zero/negative rates (22–31% zeros), but the ordering and the widening dollar pattern persist.

## Table 5 — Asset components, median among owners (secondary)

Vehicle and items>$500 medians are consistently ordered white > Black > Hispanic in all waves (e.g., 1996 vehicles: $10,000 / $8,000 / $7,000). Residential property and farm/business medians among owners are similar across cohorts (owners are selected: e.g., 1996 residential $98,000 / $90,000 / $65,000), implying the wealth gap is driven mostly by *ownership/access to assets* (who owns a home or business at all) rather than by large differences in value conditional on owning. Component counts are small and design-missing (only owners asked), so this is supporting context only.

## Attrition diagnostics
- Missingness: 1985: Black 15.1 / Hispanic 17.1 / nonBNH 23.1%; 1990: 23.7 / 23.4 / 28.9%; 1996: 31.7 / 33.4 / 52.6%.
- Stayers-vs-dropout check: 1985 median wealth of those still observed in 1996 ($1,900) is similar to those dropping out by 1996 ($2,400) — modest selection, and the balanced-panel result confirms the gap widening is not attrition-driven.

## Top-coding
Identical repeated maxima confirm top-coding: 1,054,132 (16 obs, 1985), 1,321,099 (84 obs, 1990), 1,232,183 (141 obs, 1996). Medians are unaffected; means are slightly downward-biased for the top tail.

## Workflow executed
Read data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 × 61); mapped cohort labels; computed per-wave available-case medians, means, negative/zero shares by cohort; computed dollar gaps and white-referenced ratios; balanced-panel (all-three-waves) medians; positives-only sensitivity; component medians among owners; attrition rates and stayer/dropout comparison; top-code counts. All outputs in results_log.txt and nls_wealth_results.xlsx (5 sheets). Script: analysis_nls_wealth.py.

## Limitations (restated)
(1) Cohort 3 = non-Black non-Hispanic, used as "white" proxy (includes other non-Black/non-Hispanic groups). (2) Unweighted sample medians; Sample ID confirms Black/Hispanic oversamples and a poor-white oversample within cohort 3, so results are not population-representative without survey weights, which are absent from the file. (3) Differential 1996 attrition (52.6% cohort-3 missing) — mitigated by balanced-panel check but not eliminated. (4) Family-level (respondent/spouse household) wealth, not individual. (5) "1985 onwards" is limited to the three wealth waves present (1985, 1990, 1996); 1996 is the key data point per its label.

payload.hypothesis: Median family net wealth of non-Black non-Hispanic ('white'-proxy) NLSY79 respondents exceeded that of Black and Hispanic respondents in every wealth wave from 1985 onward, and the disparity widened sharply: white/Black median ratio rose from 2.2x (1985: $3,500 vs $1,600) to 4.4x (1996: $42,600 vs $9,800), and white/Hispanic from 7.0x ($500) to 16.6x ($2,562); dollar gaps grew ~10-fold to $32,800 (Black) and $40,038 (Hispanic). The widening pattern is robust to a balanced-panel (all three waves) sensitivity and a positives-only median, and is not driven by negative/zero net worth or attrition direction. Caveats: cohort 3 is non-Black non-Hispanic, not strictly white; medians are unweighted sample medians (Black/Hispanic oversamples, no survey weights in file); 1996 missingness is high and differential (52.6% for cohort 3), though the balanced panel supports the conclusion; wealth is family/household-level; extreme wealth is top-coded (affects means, not medians).
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 respondents, 61 vars). Verified racial/ethnic cohort (1=Black n=2002, 2=Hispanic n=3174, 3=non-Black non-Hispanic n=7510) and Sample ID codes mapping perfectly to cohorts (cross-sectional + poor-white oversample + military within cohort 3; Hispanic and Black oversamples otherwise). Primary analysis: unweighted available-case medians of Family net wealth for 1985/1990/1996 by cohort, with dollar gaps and white-referenced ratios; negatives/zeros kept. Sensitivities: balanced panel (n=5,739 observed in all waves) and positives-only medians. Supporting: asset-component medians among owners; attrition diagnostics (per-wave missingness, stayer/dropout 1985 medians); top-code checks. Outputs: analysis_nls_wealth.py, results_log.txt, nls_wealth_results.xlsx (5 sheets).
